title: Emergency Funds
summary: Decide what belongs, build a layered target, choose a safe home and create a rebuild plan.
subtitle: An Emergency Fund Needs a Job Description. Otherwise, Every Surprise Applies for the Position.

blocks.text: An emergency fund is money set aside for big, sudden, unplanned needs.
It is not a general savings account, a guilt account or a tiny museum where money must sit untouched forever.

This lesson works like emergency triage. You will decide which expenses belong and build your target in small layers. Then you will pick a safe, easy-to-reach home for the money and make a rebuild plan for the day the fund does exactly what it was hired to do.
FCAC: Setting up an emergency fund

FCAC separates emergencies from occasional expenses. A car repair, urgent vet visit, job loss or health issue may qualify. School supplies, winter tires and holidays are predictable costs that belong in the budget.
Welcome to Emergency Triage
Ask these four questions before reaching for the fund. A strong emergency usually earns four convincing answers.

items.title: SUDDEN
items.text: Could you have known about this cost, or planned for it, earlier?

items.title: NECESSARY
items.text: Does it protect your health, your home, your income or a basic need?

items.title: UNPLANNED
items.text: Was it missing from your budget and your sinking funds?

items.title: TIME-SENSITIVE
items.text: Would waiting cause serious harm, a bigger cost or loss of something you need?

items.title: “Anything that feels surprising is an emergency.”
items.text: Feelings are useful alarms, but they are not a way to sort an expense. A yearly fee can feel rude when it arrives. It is still predictable, and a sinking fund should be ready for it.

blocks.text: A clear job description for your savings stops every surprise bill from raiding the same account.
blocks.detail: Four quick questions tell you whether an expense earns emergency-fund money or belongs in its own sinking fund.
blocks.extra: The triage test ahead sorts real emergencies from costs that just feel urgent.

sections.title: The Triage Board: Emergency or Sinking Fund?

blocks.text: A sinking fund is money saved gradually for a cost you know is coming.
It prevents predictable expenses from competing with true emergencies.
Emergency
Use when the cost is: Sudden, necessary, unplanned and time-sensitive.

items.title: EMERGENCY — Transmission failure
items.text: Sudden and necessary — Ask before deciding: Is the vehicle required for work or essential travel?

items.title: EMERGENCY — Urgent dental treatment
items.text: Necessary and cannot wait — Ask before deciding: What portion is not covered by insurance?

items.title: EMERGENCY — Temporary loss of income
items.text: Threatens essentials — Ask before deciding: Which essential costs must the fund carry first?

blocks.text: Sinking fund
Plan ahead when the cost is: Known, seasonal, recurring or easy to predict.

items.title: SINKING FUND — December gifts
items.text: Expected yearly — Ask before deciding: How much can be set aside monthly?

items.title: SINKING FUND — Winter tires
items.text: Seasonal and predictable — Ask before deciding: What is the replacement date and target?

items.title: SINKING FUND — Annual professional fee
items.text: Known renewal — Ask before deciding: How many months remain before it is due?

blocks.text: TRIAGE RULE
Predictable costs still need a plan, and true emergencies still deserve care.
Sorting the cost tells you which savings tool should do the work.

items.title: “If a bill arrives only once a year, it is automatically unexpected.”
items.text: A yearly licence, insurance bill or holiday comes around only once a year, but you can still plan for it and split it into monthly sinking-fund transfers.

blocks.text: The emergency fund protects the household from shocks. Sinking funds protect the emergency fund from the calendar.
Meet Jane
paragraphs: Jane lives in Fredericton and drives to early hospital shifts, so her car has one job: start every morning. In January it fails. A $720 alternator repair and tow bill lands the same week she remembers $480 of winter tires and a $240 yearly professional fee. All three act like emergencies. Jane has $900 in her emergency fund and one nervous eyebrow.

Jane runs each cost through the four questions. The alternator failure was sudden, needed for her shifts and missing from the budget, and waiting would cost her income. It passes all four. The tires and the fee are real costs, but she has known both dates for months, so they belong in sinking funds.

Paying $720 leaves Jane with $180, which looks thin next to a tank of gas and a grocery list. She thinks about the credit card in her wallet, since plastic would keep her savings looking untouched. Then she stops herself. A fund that looks full but never gets used is not protecting anyone. She pays the mechanic from savings.

She restarts her transfer at $45 every two weeks, and sixteen deposits will rebuild the $720. She also opens two sinking funds, $40 a month for tires and $20 for the fee, so next January does not try out for the emergency role again.

By the next payday, Jane has paid a real emergency without a credit card, and two costs that used to ambush her have their own accounts. Her fund is smaller, but it did what it was hired to do. Her eyebrow, for the record, has relaxed.

blocks.text: Jane paid a $720 emergency from savings, skipped the credit card and has a sixteen-payday plan to refill the fund.
blocks.detail: The same triage test and sinking-fund split can protect your own account the next time three bills land in one week.
blocks.extra: Section 03 turns that rebuild into a repeatable three-layer target.

sections.title: Build the Fund in Three Layers

items.title: STARTER SHIELD
items.text: Pick a first goal you can reach and repeat. $500 is a common example, but your number should fit your risks and your budget.

items.title: ONE MONTH OF ESSENTIALS
items.text: Add only what keeps the basics running: housing, food, transportation, insurance, medication and minimum payments.

items.title: THREE TO SIX MONTHS OF RESILIENCE
items.text: Stretch the goal to fit how steady your income is, how many people depend on it, your health and other real risks.

blocks.text: FCAC calls three to six months of regular expenses or income an ideal target. It also tells people to start with a realistic amount and save a little at a time. The ladder gives both ideas a place.

items.title: “If I cannot save three to six months now, there is no point starting.”
items.text: A smaller first layer can cover part or all of a shock and cut how much you need to borrow. Progress helps long before you reach the final target.

blocks.text: Calculate the Essential-Expense Ladder
This made-up household uses only essential monthly costs, not every purchase, to set its range.
Essential monthly baseline: $3,500. This is what it takes to keep this household’s core needs running for one month.
Protected plan: 4 categories.

items.title: Housing and utilities
items.text: $1,800 / month — Essential — 51% of essential month — Planning question: What must still be paid if income stops?

items.title: Food and household basics
items.text: $650 / month — Essential — 19% of essential month — Planning question: How low could this go in a tight month?

items.title: Transport, insurance and medication
items.text: $700 / month — Essential — 20% of essential month — Planning question: Which of these keep you working and healthy?

items.title: Required minimum payments
items.text: $350 / month — Essential obligation — 10% of essential month — Planning question: Which payments must stay up to date?

blocks.text: TARGET RANGE
$3,500 for one month; $10,500 for three months; $21,000 for six months.
These are planning points, not a pass-or-fail test.
Turn the Target into Paydays
WORKING FORMULA
(Target − current emergency savings) ÷ transfer per payday = number of deposits needed.
Plan your paydays
blocks.extra: Enter your target, what you have saved so far and what you can move each payday. Watch the number of deposits update.

blocks.text: $45 every two weeks creates $1,170 over 26 paydays. Automatic transfers can move the money before it is invited to become something else.
FCAC: Setting up an emergency fund

sections.title: Give the Fund a Safe, Usable Home

blocks.text: The best home is usually boring in the most helpful way. It should be easy to reach, separate from everyday spending, low or no fee, free of withdrawal penalties, stable in value and, where possible, earning interest.

items.title: Check access.
items.text: Know how quickly money can move, whether holds apply and whether weekend or holiday access differs.

items.title: Check the full fee schedule.
items.text: Review transfer, withdrawal, minimum-balance and transaction fees before choosing the account.

items.title: Check protection.
items.text: Ask the official insurer to confirm your bank, your product and how the account is owned. Check the current coverage rules too.

items.title: Avoid sharp market risk.
items.text: Money you may need fast should not depend on selling something that has lost value.

blocks.text: FCAC: Savings accounts

items.title: “The account with the highest possible return is always the best emergency-fund home.”
items.text: Return matters, but access, fees, stability and protection come first. A high rate does not help if withdrawals are limited, fees eat the gain or the product can drop sharply when you need cash.

blocks.text: CDIC automatically protects eligible deposits at member institutions. Coverage goes up to $100,000 in each insurance category, including principal and interest. Mutual funds, stocks, bonds, ETFs and cryptocurrencies are not covered by CDIC.

sections.title: Province Lens: Verify the Institution, Not Just the Logo

items.title: AB and BC
items.text: Provincial credit-union systems currently guarantee 100% of eligible deposits. A federal credit union in BC uses CDIC instead.

items.title: NB and PEI
items.text: NBCUDIC and PEI CUDIC protect eligible member deposits under provincial rules. Check the current limits and which accounts qualify.

items.title: ON
items.text: FSRA currently covers up to $250,000 of eligible non-registered credit-union deposits. Eligible registered deposits have no dollar limit.

items.title: NL
items.text: CUDGCNL guarantees credit-union deposits in the province. Confirm current coverage with them before choosing a product.

sections.title: Quick Check: Where Does It Go?

items.title: Urgent dental treatment that cannot safely wait.
Temporary job loss threatens rent and groceries.
Annual pet vaccination.
items.detail: Predictable care fund; urgent unplanned surgery may be an emergency.

items.title: A one-day electronics sale labelled ‘emergency pricing.’
items.detail: Not an emergency. The television will recover.

blocks.text: Before You Open the Triage File

items.title: “Using the emergency fund means I failed to protect it.”
items.text: Using the fund for a true emergency is success, not failure. Record what happened, protect your essentials right now, and start a small rebuild. Guilt is not an interest-bearing account.

blocks.text: Make the rebuild plan before you withdraw. Record the amount, restart a small automatic transfer, send any windfalls or freed-up debt payments to the gap, and start a sinking fund if the cost turns out to be predictable.

Emergency-Fund Readiness Checklist

items.title: The job is defined.
items.text: Real emergencies and predictable costs are written down in plain words.

items.title: The target has layers.
items.text: A first goal you can reach leads to one month, then to your own three-to-six-month range.

items.title: The money is usable.
items.text: The account is separate, stable and easy to reach, and you understand it before a crisis hits.

items.title: Protection is verified.
items.text: You checked the insurer’s website for your bank, product and account type.

items.title: The rebuild is automatic.
items.text: A repeating transfer and a review date start after any withdrawal for a real emergency.

blocks.text: A useful emergency fund has a clear job and a realistic layered target.
blocks.detail: It also needs a safe, easy-to-reach home, automatic deposits and a rebuild plan that starts after the fund covers a real shock.

blocks.text: An emergency fund earns its keep twice: first when it stops a shock from becoming costly debt, and again when you calmly rebuild it for the next one.

items.title: Emergency fund
items.text: Money set aside for big, sudden needs that fall outside your regular budget.

items.title: Sinking fund
items.text: Money saved a little at a time for an expense you know is coming.

items.title: Essential expense
items.text: A cost that protects housing, food, health, income or basic day-to-day life.

items.title: Starter shield
items.text: A first savings goal you can reach quickly, set before the bigger long-term target.

items.title: Resilience target
items.text: A bigger savings goal, often based on several months of essential or regular costs.

items.title: Liquidity
items.text: How fast and easily you can get at your money without losing value or paying a penalty.

items.title: Principal
items.text: The original amount of money deposited, before interest.

items.title: Interest
items.text: Money paid on savings or charged on borrowed money, usually shown as a rate.

items.title: Deposit insurance
items.text: Protection for eligible deposits if a bank or credit union fails, under the insurer’s rules.

items.title: Eligible deposit
items.text: A deposit product that meets the deposit insurer’s coverage rules.

items.title: CDIC
items.text: The federal Crown corporation that insures eligible deposits at member banks.

items.title: Automatic transfer
items.text: A scheduled move of money between accounts on a chosen date or cycle.

quiz.question: True or False: “Anything that feels surprising is an emergency.”

questions: Name one cost that is a true emergency and one that is not.
What do your essentials cost in a typical month? Think housing, food, utilities, transportation, insurance, medication and minimum payments. An estimate is fine.
What is your first savings goal, and how much would you like to reach later?
Which bank or credit union account will hold the fund? Check that deposit insurance covers it.
How much will you move to the fund each payday, and when will you check your progress?
If you use the fund, how will you refill it? Name the amount and the date you will start.
